Harlem, New York. A neighborhood in upper Manhattan that emerged as the cultural and political capital of African American life in the twentieth century. Home to the Harlem Renaissance of the nineteen-twenties and a crucial base for Civil Rights leadership, Harlem produced generations of musicians, writers, activists, and elected officials who shaped American culture. As a densely concentrated center of Black American political power, it became the electoral district for major figures like Adam Clayton Powell Junior and Charles Rangel.

Harlem rapidly transformed from a middle-class German and Jewish neighborhood into a predominantly African American enclave after nineteen-ten as racial restrictive covenants pushed Black migration northward. It became the epicenter of the Harlem Renaissance from the nineteen-twenties through the nineteen-thirties, a flourishing of jazz, blues, literature, and visual arts that redefined African American cultural identity. The neighborhood hosted vibrant nightclubs like the Cotton Club, which ironically was segregated despite hosting Black performers, and the Apollo Theater. These venues became centers of artistic innovation and audience gathering.

Harlem served as the political base for Adam Clayton Powell, who represented Harlem in Congress and wielded his electoral mandate to pressure national civil rights agendas. However, starting from the nineteen-sixties onward, Harlem experienced severe economic decline and disinvestment, with redlining and suburbanization draining wealth and opportunity. Yet the neighborhood remains symbolically central to African American identity and continues to be a site of cultural production and historical memory. The boundaries of Harlem are roughly defined as one hundred tenth to one hundred fifty-fifth Street, from the Hudson River to the East River.
